issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' is hard to reconcile with a stalking trauma in the absence of any indication that other people died or were put at comparable lethal risk. For this trauma type, that appraisal is clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste trigger is not impossible, but for stalking it lacks support from the rest of the profile: there are no memory items or contextual details suggesting an event involving gustatory cues. Given the formulation also has no Triggers ↔ Memory linkage, this trigger is clinically unsupported and difficult to explain in this profile.

vignette: Thomas, a 32-year-old European-American man, has been struggling with intense anxiety and fear since his traumatic experience of being stalked over several months. The stalking culminated in an incident where Thomas was followed to his home by someone he suspected was the stalker. During this time, the individual would send threatening messages and make calls late at night, often expressing anger that seemed directed specifically at him. This experience has left Thomas with a heightened sense of threat and pervasive distrust. Thomas's triggers are deeply embedded in his daily life. The sound of motorcycle noise, for instance, instantly brings back memories of when he heard the stalker's motorcycle approaching while he was walking home late one night. He recalls feeling petrified as the bike followed him closely, its engine roaring ominously in the darkness. Even now, any motorbike passing by on the street can cause his heart to race and his palms to sweat. Another trigger is other people expressing anger, even calmly. Thomas vividly remembers a time when he was at home alone, and the stalker had called, their voice dripping with rage. That experience has made him hyper-aware of any signs of anger from others. Recently, while teaching a class, a student raised his voice in frustration over a difficult concept, and Thomas found himself immediately feeling on edge, unable to concentrate or maintain composure. Feeling followed or tracked is another potent trigger for Thomas. He recalls walking home one night when he saw someone watching him from across the street. His heart pounded as he quickened his pace, but the figure stayed in view. This experience has left him constantly vigilant and wary of anyone who seems to be observing him. Recently, while taking a walk with his wife in a familiar park near their house, Thomas felt unnerved by someone walking behind them. He couldn't shake off the feeling that he was being followed again. Thomas's coping mechanisms have also shifted significantly since the stalking incident. He often tells himself that he deserves to suffer for what happened, believing that there must be something inherently wrong with him to attract such a stalker. This self-punishing thought has made it difficult for Thomas to seek help or even enjoy his hobbies and interests. His relationship with his wife has also been affected by these maladaptive strategies. Thomas avoids being emotionally close or intimate with her, fearing that he might bring the same danger into their lives again. He struggles to relax because it feels dangerous; instead of enjoying moments of peace, he often finds himself on high alert, scanning for any signs of threat. Thomas's avoidance behaviors have extended to his daily life and work as a tutor. He avoids going to unfamiliar places because he cannot assess the danger. For instance, he recently declined an invitation from colleagues to visit a new coffee shop down the street, citing that it was too risky to go somewhere unknown. This behavior has led him to isolate himself further, impacting both his professional and personal life. Sleep problems have also become increasingly severe for Thomas. He often lies awake at night, mind racing with thoughts of being stalked again. His wife has noticed his difficulty in falling asleep and staying asleep, which has added to the strain on their relationship. Thomas experiences frequent false alarms, reacting as if he is in danger even when nothing is actually wrong. A sudden noise outside or an unexpected shadow in a dimly lit room can trigger intense fear responses. He admits that this heightened sense of threat has made it difficult for him to engage fully with his surroundings. The negative appraisals have deeply influenced Thomas's outlook on life. He struggles with self-doubt, constantly questioning whether he will do the right thing and if he is capable of making sound decisions. This mistrust extends to others as well; he believes that people are not what they seem, and that they cannot be trusted. These beliefs have made it difficult for Thomas to form close relationships or even trust his own judgment. What finally brought Thomas to seek help was the realization that these fears were increasingly isolating him from those around him. He feared losing his wife and the life he had built due to his constant state of hypervigilance and avoidance. While he is scared about what might happen if he confronts these fears, he is most hopeful for a sense of safety and trust again in his daily life.
